clue.text: A craftsman — though this could turn out to be a trick name

indicators.note: to turn out can mean to come out differently, so the following words are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A skilled woodworker's job title is said to conceal a conjuror's stage name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn out' rearranges the ten letters of BE A TRICK NAME; 'though this could' and 'to' only join the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of fine wooden furniture such as cupboards and chests is a skilled artisan.

clue.text: Collapse of first-rate horseman

parts.note: crack means top-class, as in a crack shot
in racing a jockey is said to be up when riding a horse

explanation.surface: A top-class rider takes a fall.
explanation.walkthrough: Racecards say 'X up' for the jockey riding, so a horseman is UP.
explanation.definitionFit: A breakdown, physical or mental, is a sudden failure of strength.

clue.text: One of the doggy tribe, maybe

definitions.text: One of the doggy tribe, maybe

parts.words: One of the doggy tribe, maybe
parts.note: a dog that snaps at people is described by what it does with its teeth

explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' admits that not every dog does it; the clue describes a snappy animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog that snaps with its teeth is one that nips.

clue.text: Little William's evening wear

parts.note: Wee Willie Winkie of the nursery rhyme runs through the town in his bedtime garment

explanation.walkthrough: Evening wear suggests a dinner jacket; Little William is Wee Willie Winkie, the nursery-rhyme boy who runs 'upstairs and downstairs' in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A long loose garment worn in bed is what one wears at night.

clue.text: Bit upset — it's a trick!

indicators.note: upset means turned over, and in a down clue that turns the word bit upside down

parts.note: a part is a bit of something

explanation.surface: Someone is a little distressed to find they have been fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns PART upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A snare set to catch someone out is a ruse.

clue.text: Painstaking hostile warrior

indicators.note: taking means swallowing up, so the word for pains takes in another word

parts.note: aches are pains
ill as in ill will, unfriendly

explanation.surface: A meticulous fighter is unfriendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Painstaking' splits into 'Pains' (ACHES) and 'taking', which puts ILL inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek hero of the Trojan War was the greatest fighter at Troy.

clue.text: Last verse delivered in a golden voice

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit within the words a golden voice

explanation.surface: A closing stanza is sung by a richly toned singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivered in' points into golDEN VOIce.
explanation.definitionFit: A short closing stanza of a ballade addresses the poem's patron.

clue.text: Bugs caught inside are a bit messy

indicators.note: inside means the letter for caught goes within the mixed-up letters
messy means jumbled and untidy, so the letters of are a bit are scrambled

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Insects trapped indoors make things a little untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'messy' rearranges ARE A BIT into BATERIA, and 'inside' puts C into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Germs that cause illness are colloquially called bugs.

clue.text: Mounted police covered by curious set of orders

indicators.note: covered by means wrapped inside, so the police letters sit within the other letters
curious means odd, so the letters of set are rearranged
mounted means going up, and in a down clue that reads the police letters upward

parts.note: CID, the Criminal Investigation Department

explanation.surface: Mounted officers are hidden among a strange group of commands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curious' rearranges SET into ETS; 'Mounted' turns CID upwards into DIC, which 'covered by' places inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Edicts are official decrees, commands issued by authority.

clue.text: Sign-writing by me

parts.note: read literally, a self-written signature: Greek auto means self and graph means writing

explanation.walkthrough: Sign-writing suggests painting shop fronts, but the sign here is a signature written by one's own hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A signature in a person's own handwriting is literally self-writing, from the Greek roots for self and write.

clue.text: Provision for the old road to Central London

parts.note: via is Latin for road, the language of the Romans' old roads

indicators.note: central asks for the letters in the very middle of the word London

explanation.surface: Supplies are sent along an ancient route into the heart of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central' takes the middle pair of LONDON, N and D.
explanation.definitionFit: A viand is an item of food, and provisions are stores of food.

clue.text: Artist in the clutches of a shrew gets the chop perhaps

indicators.note: being held in someone's clutches means being gripped inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Kate is the shrew of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew
RA, a Royal Academician, is a standard crossword artist

explanation.surface: A painter caught by a nagging woman ends up being dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the chop' looks like being sacked; instead the chop is a blow from a martial art.
explanation.definitionFit: A chop delivered with the edge of the hand is a signature blow of this Japanese martial art.

clue.text: Like the Mikado's billiard balls a novice missed

definitions.text: Like the Mikado's billiard balls a novice missed

indicators.note: something missed is left out, so these letters are dropped from the longer word

parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado the billiard sharp is condemned to play with elliptical billiard balls
L, the learner plate, stands for a novice

explanation.surface: A beginner fails to hit the misshapen balls from a comic opera's punishment song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missed' drops A and L from ELLIPTICAL; the shorter word means the same oval shape, so the whole clue defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both forms describe an oval shape, which is what the opera's misshapen balls are.

clue.text: He has finished, or is in a leading position

definitions.text: He has finished, or is in a leading position

parts.note: something finished is over and done, in the past

explanation.surface: Someone has either retired or is still at the head of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: PAST plus OR; the whole clue also describes a clergyman, who leads a flock.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister leads a congregation, so he stands at the head of his flock.

clue.text: Close throttle — street takes a 90 turn

parts.note: a ninety-degree turn is a right angle, with right abbreviated to R

explanation.surface: Shutting the engine's throttle, a car swings round a corner on a road.
explanation.walkthrough: A 90-degree turn is a right angle, R ANGLE with 'right' shortened to R; 'takes' just joins. 'Close throttle' looks like engine talk but means grip the throat.
explanation.definitionFit: To choke someone is to squeeze the throat shut.

clue.text: Hamite is a prickly specimen

parts.note: the Berbers of North Africa were classed as a Hamitic people

explanation.surface: A North African tribesman is described as a thorny character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamite' is an old ethnological label for peoples such as the Berbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Barberry is a spiny shrub, so any plant of this genus is a thorny example.

clue.text: Account by native no good — the water is stagnant

definitions.note: the definition is a description of a backwater rather than a noun phrase

parts.note: a bill is an account of money owed
Abo is an old, now offensive, Australian term for an Aboriginal person

explanation.surface: An Aboriginal's report says the pond has gone stale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia a cut-off pool or backwater left by a river holds still, unmoving water.

clue.text: At Headingley, perhaps, the little lad swore

parts.note: Headingley in Leeds is a Test match cricket ground, standing for a Test
Ed is a short form of a boy's name such as Edward

explanation.surface: At a Yorkshire cricket match, a small boy used bad language.
explanation.walkthrough: HEADINGLEY is a Leeds cricket ground that stages Test matches; 'the' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to declare under oath, so swore is its past sense.

clue.text: Note on place for vessels to soak

parts.note: a marina is a harbour where boats moor
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A notice at a harbour warns that boats are about to get drenched.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' places the note after MARINA.
explanation.definitionFit: To steep food in a seasoned liquid is to let it absorb, or steep, before cooking.

clue.text: Doctor, shipwrecked, inclined to be gloomy

parts.note: MO, a medical officer
read as ship wrecked: the letters of ship broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A medic washed up after a wreck tends to feel low.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'shipwrecked' into 'ship' and 'wrecked': the word ship, rearranged, gives PISH after MO.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who mopes is listless and dejected, given to low spirits.

clue.text: A record bill to put before a wool-producer

parts.note: LP, a long-playing record
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: Someone advises filing a disc and an invoice ahead of a sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to put before' just lines the pieces up in order.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American relative of the llama is farmed for its fine fleece.

clue.text: A senior officer, yet mistaken for an attendant

parts.note: Col, colonel

indicators.note: mistaken means wrong, so the letters of yet are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A high-ranking officer was wrongly taken for a servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistaken' rearranges YET into YTE.
explanation.definitionFit: An acolyte is an assistant at a church service, a follower or helper.

clue.text: Aid to look-out on the bridge

definitions.text: Aid to look-out on the bridge

parts.words: Aid to look-out on the bridge
parts.note: the bridge is not a ship's but the bridge of the nose, where clip-on spectacles perch

explanation.walkthrough: The ship's lookout on the bridge is a decoy; these spectacles grip the bridge of the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles without arms that clip onto the nose help their wearer see.

clue.text: The sphere of a mother

parts.note: the planet is the globe personified as Mother of all living things

explanation.walkthrough: A mother's sphere suggests the home; the sphere is our planet, called Mother in the phrase for nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Our planet is a globe, personified in the phrase about nature as a parent.

clue.text: Cowboy developing a cough

indicators.note: developing means growing into a new shape, so the letters of a cough are reorganised

explanation.surface: A cattleman comes down with a chest complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developing' rearranges A COUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaucho is a South American horseman who herds cattle on the pampas.

clue.text: Makers of song sheets, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word for sheets is spoken rather than written

parts.note: a quire is a set of twenty-four or twenty-five sheets of paper

explanation.surface: Song sheets are produced, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Song sheets' is a false pairing: 'Makers of song' defines, and sheets give a paper term spoken aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: A body of singers produces music together, as in a church.

clue.text: Dance in a kind of circle

definitions.text: Dance in a kind of circle

parts.words: Dance in a kind of circle
parts.note: a Hawaiian dance whose name also labels a plastic hoop swung round the waist

explanation.walkthrough: The kind of circle is a hoop named after this Hawaiian dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hawaiian dance gave its name to the toy hoop whirled round the hips.

clue.text: This system perhaps also runs us

annotationWithheld.why: This system perhaps also runs us (5): SOLAR is ALSO + R rearranged, but 'runs' would have to be both R and the anagram signal, and 'us' does no job
annotationWithheld.clue: This system perhaps also runs us

clue.text: Varied form of words for redundancy

definitions.text: Varied form of words for redundancy

parts.words: Varied form of words for redundancy
parts.note: saying the same thing again in different words is needless repetition

explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes the fault itself: repeating an idea in another wording adds nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Needless repetition of an idea in other words is a stylistic fault of excess.

clue.text: West Country stuff is passable though it has holes in it

definitions.text: West Country stuff is passable though it has holes in it

parts.words: West Country stuff is passable though it has holes in it
parts.note: the cheese from Somerset suggests the first word, and a ravine you can pass through, riddled with caves, suggests the second

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a review of cheese; in fact it is a Somerset ravine, a pass full of caves. The West Country is south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: This limestone ravine in Somerset is a famous pass through the Mendips, honeycombed with caves.
